# Results — Study 915 (K-1 vs 1099) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Two wrappers around the same
commodity beta: **DBC** (Invesco DB Commodity Index Tracking Fund — a commodity pool that
issues a **Schedule K-1**, futures gains taxed under **Section 1256**) against **PDBC**
(Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy **No K-1** ETF — a 1940-Act fund
whose futures live in a Cayman subsidiary, so it issues a **Form 1099**). Both are held
buy-and-hold; both are measured **excess of cash** (minus BIL's total return) so the
collateral T-bill yield — which reached ~5%/yr in 2023-2026 — is netted out of both sides.
Daily **total-return** closes (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`; distributions reinvested,
which matters here because PDBC's ordinary distributions are large in high-rate years).
Common PDBC∩DBC∩BIL window 2014-11-07 → 2026-06-30 (PDBC's inception gates the start).
As-of **2026-06-30** — the partial current month is dropped, and the annual after-tax model
uses only the eleven **complete** calendar years 2015-2025.*

**One execution lag, and only one.** Nothing is timed: the wrapper is chosen once, bought at
the close of the first common session, and the first return counted is the following
session's. **No shorting anywhere**, so no borrow cost arises.

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| PDBC (1099), DBC (K-1), BIL (cash) | 2014-11-07 → 2026-06-30 | 2,926 | Fingerprint `0e33b87210d5` |

Context vehicles also cached: **USCI**, **USO**, **BNO** (all K-1 partnerships).

## Layer 1 — the pre-tax race (pure tape, nothing assumed)

| Wrapper | Excess Sharpe | CAGR | Vol | Max drawdown | HAC *t* (mean) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **PDBC** — Form 1099 | **+0.151** | +3.01% | 18.1% | −49.3% | +0.51 |
| **DBC** — Schedule K-1 | **+0.159** | +3.16% | 17.9% | −50.6% | +0.53 |

- **Annualised return difference (1099 − K-1): −0.1274%/yr** (−0.0506 bp/day), **HAC
  *t* = −0.21**. Paired block-bootstrap 95% CI **[−1.03%, +0.78%]**/yr, P(<0) = 0.62.
- **Excess-of-cash Sharpe advantage: −0.0081**, paired bootstrap CI **[−0.059, +0.042]** —
  a much tighter interval than bootstrapping each Sharpe separately would give, because
  resampling the *same* dates on both legs cancels the shared commodity beta.
- Correlation **0.957**, beta **0.963**, R² **0.915**.
- The **fee gap is a PROXY**, not a measurement: prospectus expense ratios DBC 0.87% vs
  PDBC 0.59% predict the 1099 wrapper should win by **+28 bp/yr**. It actually lost by
  13 bp/yr — a ~41 bp/yr shortfall that is comfortably inside one standard error
  (HAC 61 bp/yr), i.e. the tape cannot tell the fee prediction apart from zero.
  *Hindsight labelled:* these are the **current** prospectus ratios applied to the whole
  2014-2026 window. They are never subtracted from any return series — both tapes are
  already net of the real, time-varying fees — so the hindsight touches only this
  prediction-vs-tape sentence, never a backtest.

## Is that 5.3% tracking error economic — or microstructure?

| Measured at | Difference | Tracking error | HAC *t* | lag-1 autocorr |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Daily (√252-scaled) | −0.127%/yr | **5.30%/yr** | −0.21 | **−0.430** |
| Monthly (140 months) | −0.195%/yr | **1.46%/yr** | −0.68 | −0.421 |

The daily difference has a lag-1 autocorrelation of **−0.43**: the two closes disagree,
then re-converge the next session. That is premium/discount and print-timing noise, not
divergence a holder lives through — measured monthly the tracking error collapses from
5.30% to **1.46%/yr**. This also explains why the HAC and bootstrap standard errors are
three times smaller than the naive i.i.d. one.

## How large a wrapper cost could this sample have caught?

| Standard error of the annual difference | SE | Minimum detectable at \|*t*\| = 2 |
|---|--:|--:|
| Naive i.i.d. | 1.56%/yr | 3.11%/yr |
| HAC (Newey-West) | 0.61%/yr | **1.22%/yr** |
| Block bootstrap (21-day) | 0.45%/yr | **0.91%/yr** |

A null is only worth reporting when the test could have rejected. This one could: any
wrapper cost above roughly **0.9-1.2%/yr** would have shown up. The honest statement is
therefore "**no wrapper cost larger than about 1%/yr**", not "no wrapper cost".

## Robustness — two eras (split 2021-01-01)

| Era | n | Difference (*t*) | TE (daily √252-scaled) | K-1 exSharpe → 1099 exSharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2014-11 → 2020-12 | 1,547 | **+0.008%**/yr (*t* = +0.01) | 7.04% | −0.327 → −0.321 |
| 2021-01 → 2026-06 | 1,377 | **−0.319%**/yr (*t* = −0.73) | 2.00% | +0.639 → +0.624 |

Null in **both** halves. The tracking error has *fallen* from 7.04% to 2.00%/yr as PDBC
grew out of its illiquid first years — the wrappers have converged, not diverged. (Both
era TEs are the naive √252-scaled daily figure, which the section above shows overstates
the divergence a holder lives through; the fall between eras is the point, not the level.)

| 2019 | +11.44% | +11.84% | −0.40 pp | +2.03% |
| 2020 | −7.84% | −7.84% | −0.01 pp | +0.40% |
| 2021 | +41.72% | +41.36% | **+0.36 pp** | −0.10% |
| 2022 | +19.23% | +19.34% | −0.11 pp | +1.40% |
| 2023 | −6.25% | −6.19% | −0.05 pp | +4.94% |
| 2024 | +2.09% | +2.18% | −0.09 pp | +5.19% |
| 2025 | +5.96% | +8.10% | **−2.14 pp** | +4.15% |

The 1099 wrapper wins **3 of 11** years (win rate 27%, Wilson 95% CI [10%, 57%] — a coin
flip is inside the interval). Nine of the eleven differences are inside ±1 pp, ten inside
±1.2 pp; the two largest (2018 −1.14 pp, 2025 −2.14 pp) are **not** decomposed by this
study. PDBC is an *actively managed* fund — it does not mechanically replicate DBC's index
— so basket drift is the natural candidate and a wrapper cost is not, but that is an
**interpretation, not a measurement**: no holdings file was parsed and the study cannot
separate the two. Note also that the outliers do not line up with any wrapper story —
the sign reverses (2015 +0.74 pp) and the years are scattered across the sample.

## Cost sensitivity — an asymmetric, punitive sweep

Both total-return series are already net of their expense ratios, and buy-and-hold means
**one round trip**, so friction is amortised over the whole holding period
(2 × spread ÷ 11.6 years).

| Extra one-way spread charged to the 1099 leg | Annual drag | Difference (*t*) | Sharpe advantage |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bp (as traded) | 0.00 bp/yr | −0.127%/yr (−0.21) | −0.0081 |
| 10 bp | 1.72 bp/yr | −0.145%/yr (−0.24) | −0.0090 |
| 25 bp | 4.31 bp/yr | −0.171%/yr (−0.28) | −0.0104 |
| 50 bp | 8.62 bp/yr | −0.214%/yr (−0.35) | −0.0128 |

Trading friction is irrelevant at this horizon: a punitive 50 bp one-way spread moves the
annual difference by 9 bp.

## Layer 3 — the after-tax MODEL (every input below is an ASSUMPTION)

Nothing in this section is measured. It applies the two tax regimes to the realised
2015-2025 annual returns under stated marginal rates:

- **K-1 leg (DBC).** Section 1256: **marked to market each 31 December** whether or not
  you sell, taxed at the **60/40 blend**; collateral interest (proxied by BIL's total
  return on the opening balance) taxed as ordinary income; net 1256 losses carried forward;
  tax paid out of the account. Annual mark-to-market steps the basis up, so **nothing is
  owed at liquidation**.
- **1099 leg (PDBC).** Ordinary distributions equal to `payout_share` × the same interest
  proxy, taxed annually and reinvested (basis rises; the tax withdrawal removes basis pro
  rata); everything else **deferred** and taxed once at the long-term rate on sale at the
  end of the sample.
- Not modelled: state tax, the accountant time a K-1 costs, K-1 filing extensions, the fact
  that PDBC is IRA-eligible while a K-1 pool can generate UBTI in one.

**After-tax gap (1099 − K-1), pp/yr:**

| Bracket (ordinary / LTCG) | 1256 blend | payout 0.0 | 0.5 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.0 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 22% / 15%, no NIIT | 0.178 | +0.168 | +0.086 | **+0.002** | −0.084 | −0.275 |
| 24% / 15%, no NIIT | 0.186 | +0.225 | +0.124 | **+0.021** | −0.085 | −0.295 |
| 35.8% / 18.8% (32% + NIIT) | 0.256 | +0.512 | +0.333 | **+0.149** | −0.040 | −0.360 |
| 40.8% / 23.8% (top + NIIT) | 0.306 | +0.588 | +0.407 | **+0.219** | +0.023 | −0.340 |

**The whole grid spans [−0.36, +0.59] pp/yr and the sign flips inside it.** The
after-tax answer is a function of the distribution-policy assumption, not of the tape:
if the 1099 fund distributes little, deferral wins; if it distributes twice the collateral
interest — which a fund of this type can do when its subsidiary realises gains — the K-1's
60/40 rate wins. **PDBC's actual payout is not measured here** (no distribution filing was
parsed), which is precisely why the grid is swept rather than evaluated at one point.

**The regime alone** — both tax rules applied to the *same* (DBC) return stream, so the
tracking difference disappears and only the tax treatment remains:

| Bracket | K-1 after-tax CAGR | 1099 after-tax CAGR | Regime gap |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 22% / 15% | +2.483% | +2.725% | **+0.241 pp/yr** |
| 24% / 15% | +2.426% | +2.686% | **+0.260 pp/yr** |
| 35.8% / 18.8% | +2.034% | +2.414% | **+0.380 pp/yr** |
| 40.8% / 23.8% | +1.818% | +2.256% | **+0.438 pp/yr** |

At `payout_share` = 1 the deferral is worth 24-44 bp/yr to the 1099 wrapper — which is,
almost exactly, what the tracking difference takes back. Pre-tax CAGR over the complete
years is +3.328% (K-1) vs +3.055% (1099); after tax at 35.8/18.8 it is +2.034% vs +2.183%.

| PDBC | 1099 | +3.01% | 18.1% | +0.151 | −49.3% |
| BNO | K-1 | +1.85% | 37.6% | +0.188 | −81.5% |
| USO | K-1 | **−6.70%** | 39.8% | −0.019 | −92.8% |

Index and vehicle choice spans **11.38 pp/yr** of CAGR over the same window. The wrapper
choice is worth **0.13 pp/yr**. The paperwork decision is roughly **90× smaller** than the
decision it is usually bundled with.

## Cross-checks

- **Synthetic control** (machinery proof only, never supports the stamp): on a pair with a
  *planted* 4.00%/yr wrapper drag the race recovers **4.95%/yr** at HAC *t* = **−4.03**; on
  eight independent null pairs (identical wrappers, tracking noise only) the mean estimated
  drift is **+0.45%/yr** (sd 1.06%) and **0/8** clear |*t*| = 2. The estimator finds a real
  wrapper cost and does not invent one.

## Verdict

- **Signal — None.** There is no detectable performance difference between the two
  wrappers. The annualised difference is **−0.127%/yr** at **HAC *t* = −0.21**, with a
  paired bootstrap CI of **[−1.03%, +0.78%]**; the excess-of-cash Sharpe advantage is
  **−0.008** with a CI of **[−0.059, +0.042]**; the difference is null in **both** eras
  (+0.01% then −0.32%, |*t*| ≤ 0.73), the 1099 wrapper wins only 3 of 11 years with a
  coin flip inside the Wilson interval, and a punitive 50 bp spread moves the answer by
  9 bp. This is an informative null rather than an underpowered one: the sample could have
  caught any cost above ~0.9-1.2%/yr. The after-tax model does not rescue a signal either —
  its gap spans [−0.36, +0.59] pp/yr and **changes sign** with the distribution-payout
  assumption, so the after-tax winner is chosen by the assumption, not by the tape.
  *Survivorship:* neither wrapper is survivorship-selected — both are the live, named
  vehicles an investor actually faced from PDBC's inception, and no dead commodity ETP was
  dropped from the comparison. But the pair itself was chosen *because* it is the famous
  K-1/No-K-1 twin, which is a selection on salience, not on performance.
  *Confound, named:* PDBC is **actively managed** and does not mechanically replicate DBC's
  index, so "legal wrapper" and "basket" cannot be separated in this pair. What is measured
  is the **joint** difference; the null therefore bounds wrapper *plus* basket drift
  together at ~1%/yr, and the two outlier years are interpreted, not decomposed.
- **Tradability — Mirage.** There is no edge to bank. The wrapper difference is tens of
  basis points against 146-530 bp/yr of tracking error and against 11.4 pp/yr of
  index-choice dispersion; the after-tax gap is smaller than the assumptions that generate
  it. The genuinely useful finding is the *non*-finding: the 1099 convenience — no Schedule
  K-1, no partnership filing extension, IRA eligibility — appears to be **free**, not paid
  for in performance. That is worth knowing, and it is not an alpha.
